title: Dark Store Crackdown Widens as Regulators Seal Zepto, Blinkit Facilities Across India
excerpt: Food safety officials in Karnataka and Maharashtra shut quick-commerce warehouses over hygiene violations, while distributors demand stricter platform accountability.
body:
• Karnataka food safety officials sealed a Zepto warehouse in Bengaluru for unhygienic conditions, improper labelling, and misbranding, while Maharashtra FDA suspended a Blinkit facility in Mumbai's Malad for cockroach infestation and expired goods.
  • The All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) questioned why Zepto is intervening to reverse the seal on a facility it claims not to own or operate.
  • AICPDF has demanded FSSAI prescribe minimum space requirements of 20,000–25,000 square feet for dark stores and called for stricter IPO scrutiny of loss-making quick-commerce companies.
  • The crackdown follows months of escalating enforcement across Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana, with over 236 dark stores inspected in a Bengaluru drive that found expired products worth over ₹2.35 lakh.

Two Facilities Shut Down in a Single Week

Quick commerce platforms Zepto and Blinkit found themselves on the wrong side of food regulators within days of each other. Karnataka's Food Safety and Drug Administration sealed a Zepto warehouse in Hoskote, on the outskirts of Bengaluru, after inspectors found unhygienic food conditions, improper labelling, misbranding, and breaches of food-handling and storage practices. In Mumbai, the Maharashtra FDA suspended the licence of a Blinkit facility in Malad West after an August 7 inspection uncovered what officials described as "extremely unhygienic" conditions.

At the Blinkit facility, inspectors found improperly stored food, inadequate cleanliness in cold storage, expired and damaged packaged goods, and violations of First-In, First-Out and First-Expired, First-Out inventory management practices. Cockroaches were discovered in the fruit and vegetable storage area. The facility's licence has been cancelled until further notice.

"This episode clearly exposes the duplicity in the business models of quick commerce platforms. You cannot claim to be just a tech enabler and then attempt to overturn regulatory action against a facility you officially don't own or operate."

— Dhairyashil Patil, National President, AICPDF

Distributors Question Platform Accountability

The All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation, which represents 4.5 lakh FMCG distributors, seized on the enforcement actions to press its case against quick-commerce business models. AICPDF flagged what it called a fundamental contradiction: despite Zepto's public claims that inventory is held by independent sellers or dark store operators, the company has been actively pursuing efforts to reverse the warehouse seal.

"If the inventory does not belong to Zepto, then on what basis is the company intervening in the regulatory process," the federation asked in a statement. AICPDF argued the platform's intervention "indirectly affirms their involvement in inventory handling, which contradicts their operational declarations."

The federation has also urged the government and SEBI to block IPOs of persistent loss-making quick-commerce companies without stricter scrutiny. It called for mandatory minimum storage norms of 20,000–25,000 square feet for dark stores, noting that many currently cram 60,000 to 70,000 SKUs into limited floor space.

A Pattern of Violations

The latest actions are part of an intensifying nationwide crackdown. In June, a two-day enforcement drive in Bengaluru inspected 236 dark stores operated by Blinkit, Amazon, Zepto, and Flipkart, seizing expired and misbranded products worth over ₹2.35 lakh and booking 44 violation cases. Notices were issued to 65 food business operators, with penalties totalling ₹1.98 lakh.

Maharashtra has been particularly aggressive. The state's FDA inspected 43 dark stores across the state, issuing 34 notices, five shutdown orders, and one licence suspension. Earlier in 2025 and 2026, individual Zepto and Blinkit facilities in Dharavi, Pune, and now Malad have been shut or had licences revoked. The FDA also recently suspended Parle Agro's licence after finding expired Frooti and Appy products at its Chembur warehouse.

The FSSAI itself has issued notices to Blinkit over consumer complaints about spoiled food delivered through the platform, and warned all e-commerce platforms to comply with labelling, shelf-life display, and hygiene regulations — or face severe consequences.

Industry Response

Zepto told MediaNama that it had cooperated with authorities during the inspection and was "taking the necessary steps to address" the observations. "We remain committed to continuously strengthening our processes and maintaining high standards of food safety and hygiene," a spokesperson said. Blinkit has not publicly responded to the Malad suspension.

The regulatory heat comes at a sensitive moment for the sector. Zepto recently shelved its IPO over valuation concerns, and the broader quick-commerce industry — which processes an estimated 9.5 million daily orders across India — faces growing scrutiny over whether its breakneck delivery speeds come at the expense of basic food safety standards.
nri_angle: For NRIs who rely on quick-commerce apps for family deliveries in India, the food safety crackdown raises questions about the safety standards behind rapid delivery services.
author: Diaspora Desk
